meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I had been pushed around all my life and felt at this moment that I couldn't take it anymore'?
meta.ogDescription: Not an interview and not a memoir: Parks’s own handwritten draft, held in the Rosa Parks Papers at the Library of Congress.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Rosa Parks wrote this herself, in pen, on a loose sheet among the drafts she made of her own account of the arrest. The sheet is in the Rosa Parks Papers at the Library of Congress ↗, in a folder the Library dates 1956–circa 1958. It is about as direct a source as this corpus ever gets: no co-author, no interviewer, no anthology in between.

source.excerpt: I had been pushed around [for] all my life [becau] and felt at this moment that I couldn’t take it anymore. When I asked the policeman why we [were] had to be pushed around? He said he didn’t know. “The law is the law. you are under arrest. [I actu] [I went will] I didn’t resist.
trail: We searched the Library of Congress’s Rosa Parks Papers ↗ for the phrase and the top result was this folder of her own draft accounts of the arrest.
We then read the Library’s volunteer transcription of the individual sheet — image 27’s plain-text file ↗ — which reproduces the sentence verbatim, including the words Parks crossed out.

The folder’s catalogue record names Parks as the sole creator and dates the drafts 1956–circa 1958, so this is a reflection written a year or two after the December 1955 arrest, not a statement made on the night.

Note on links: loc.gov returns 403 to automated requests from some networks even though the pages load normally in a browser. We verified this record through the Library’s own JSON API and its transcription files, both of which returned the same folder and sheet.
source.cutTag: Transcribed by Library of Congress “By the People” volunteers
source.excerptNote: Square brackets are the transcribers’ marks for words Parks struck out as she wrote — so the sentence in circulation is exactly the sentence she settled on. The punctuation and capitalisation are hers; the closing quotation mark is unclosed on the sheet.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.bio: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks (1913–2005) was an American civil rights activist and secretary of the Montgomery NAACP branch, work that had her collecting testimony about racial violence in Alabama for years before her own arrest. Her refusal to move on 1 December 1955 triggered the 381-day Montgomery bus boycott. Her personal papers are held by the Library of Congress.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The story most people know about 1 December 1955 has Parks too tired to stand. She spent the rest of her life saying that was wrong, and this sheet is her doing it early, in private, before anyone had turned her into a statue.

What she names instead is accumulation: not one evening’s exhaustion but a lifetime of being moved along. The next sentence on the page is her asking the arresting officer why, and being told the law is the law.
detailsBody: Parks was 42, and had been secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP since 1943 — twelve years spent investigating and organising around cases of racial and sexual violence in Alabama. A few months before the arrest she had attended the Highlander Folk School in Monteagle, Tennessee. The image of a weary seamstress acting on impulse was useful to some tellings of the boycott and irritating to her.

Her papers are at the Library of Congress on loan from the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and have been digitised, which is why a private draft like this one is readable at all. The transcription quoted above was made by volunteers through the Library’s By the People ↗ programme.
